(The Frisky) -- There exists a school of thought that dictates if you think something catastrophic, then it won't happen. What would happen if my family died in a car accident? What would happen if my house caught on fire? "What makes men connect with the girl of their dreams after sparking with me?" the author asks. Two summers ago, I asked myself: Wouldn't it suck if my first love met someone unexpectedly and got over me before I could begin to move on? Thankfully, my family and my house are safe, but my feelings, my love life, and my ego still need mending. "I met someone." The text message appeared on the screen of my phone and I stopped walking. A group of my friends and I were leaving the movie theater, and it was as if all feelings he had for me were obliterated in one night. We broke up because he was studying in Europe. Poetically, we had expressed our feelings for each other just two nights before. Then he became someone else's boyfriend, and remained so, for much longer than he and I lasted. I should've known it would happen, since it happens quite often. My first kiss, who refused to be my boyfriend, met the girl of his dreams while I still ached for him. They're still together today. Since then, I've been the second choice for several more men. The most recent ones occurred this summer, when I tried and failed to win the heart of my friend Ken -- he started dating the person that he truly liked instead of settling for me. I lost Brian to his ex-girlfriend (although, in that case, I think they belonged together anyway). Each time, I laughed one of those sad, desperate guffaws -- here we go again! What makes men connect with the girl of their dreams after sparking with me? Another concept may be more applicable to my situation: the idea of a self-fulfilling prophecy. Perhaps I'm so aware of my "magic touch" that I'm making it happen. While the first love arrived in Europe, I even warned him what may happen. At the time, though, he waved the thought away. "I'm so picky, I rarely really like a girl like I like you," he typed. A month later, he must've been pleasantly shocked to discover my unfortunate power reached across the Atlantic Ocean. When Ken told me he was dating Mary, I was angry I'd let this happen to me again. I raged at him. He argued that it's irrational to use my past experience to predict the outcome of my future relationships (or my attempts at them). I'm sure that there'll be a guy someday who doesn't find me easy to move on from, but in the meantime I can't ignore the pattern and pretend that each time was a coincidence, as Ken had wanted me to do. I don't know if there is a way to avoid the seemingly inevitable. Each time I let my hopes conquer my superstition, there's a crash, a burn, a deflation, and the temporary loss of the ability to giggle, but I choose the chance of being the girl before the girlfriend over giving up the chance for breaking my streak. outputs.L1:
(The Frisky) -- There exists a school of thought which holds that if you imagine something catastrophic, it won't come to pass. What would happen if my family perished in a car accident? What would happen if my house went up in flames? "What is it that leads men to connect with the girl of their dreams after first sparking with me?" the author asks. Two summers ago, I posed a question of my own: Wouldn't it be devastating if my first love met someone unexpectedly and moved on from me before I could even begin to heal?

Thankfully, my family and my house remain safe, yet my feelings, my love life, and my ego are still in need of mending.

"I met someone." The text message flashed across the screen of my phone, and I stopped in my tracks. A group of my friends and I were leaving the movie theater, and it was as though every feeling he had ever harbored for me had been obliterated in a single night. We had broken up because he was studying in Europe. Poetically, we had confessed our feelings for each other just two nights before. Then he became someone else's boyfriend—and remained so far longer than he and I had ever lasted.

I should have anticipated it, for such things happen to me all too often. My first kiss, who had refused to be my boyfriend, found the girl of his dreams while I still ached for him. They remain together to this day. Since then, I have been the second choice for several more men. The most recent instances unfolded this summer, when I tried—and failed—to win the heart of my friend Ken; he chose to date the person he truly desired rather than settle for me. I lost Brian to his ex-girlfriend as well (though, in that case, I believe they were meant for each other anyway). Each time, I let out one of those sad, desperate laughs—here we go again!

What is it that leads men to connect with the girl of their dreams after first sparking with me?

Perhaps another concept is more applicable to my situation: the notion of a self-fulfilling prophecy. Perhaps I am so conscious of my "magic touch" that I am the very one bringing it about. When my first love arrived in Europe, I even warned him of what might happen. At the time, however, he brushed the thought aside. "I'm so picky—I rarely truly like a girl the way I like you," he typed. A month later, he must have been pleasantly astonished to discover that my unfortunate power reached clear across the Atlantic Ocean.

When Ken told me he was dating Mary, I was furious that I had allowed this to happen to me yet again. I railed at him. He countered that it was irrational to use my past experiences to predict the outcome of my future relationships (or my attempts at them). I am certain that someday there will be a man who does not find me so easy to move on from, but in the meantime, I cannot ignore the pattern and pretend that each occurrence was mere coincidence, as Ken would have me believe.

I do not know whether there is a way to avert the seemingly inevitable. Each time I allow my hopes to conquer my superstition, there is a crash, a burn, a deflation, and the temporary loss of my ability to laugh—yet I would rather take the chance of being the girl before the girlfriend than surrender my chance of finally breaking the streak.

(The Frisky) -- Some people believe that if you imagine a disaster happening, it never actually will. What if my whole family perished in a car crash? What if flames consumed my home? "Why do men find the woman of their dreams right after being with me?" the writer wonders. Back during a summer two years ago, a different fear crossed my mind: How awful would it be if my first love stumbled into a new relationship and moved past me before I had any chance to recover myself?

Fortunately, neither my house nor my family have come to harm. But my heart, my dating life, and my self-esteem are all still in need of repair.

"I met someone." Those words popped up on my phone's screen, and I froze in my tracks. I was walking out of the movie theater with a handful of friends when, in a single evening, every ounce of affection he'd held for me seemed to vanish. Our relationship had ended because he'd gone to study overseas in Europe. What made it painfully ironic was that we had confessed our love to one another only two evenings earlier. Not long after, he was calling someone else his girlfriend -- a relationship that outlasted ours by a wide margin.

I really should have anticipated it, because this keeps repeating in my life. The boy who gave me my first kiss but refused to officially date me? He found his dream girl while I was still nursing feelings for him. They remain a couple to this day. And ever since, I've played runner-up to a string of guys.

The latest examples happened this summer. I attempted, without success, to capture the affection of my friend Ken -- rather than settling for me, he chose to date the girl he genuinely wanted. And I lost Brian back to his former girlfriend (though honestly, I think those two were always meant to be). On each occasion, I let out one of those hopeless, bitter laughs -- not this again!

Why is it that men link up with their ideal woman right after a spark with me?

Maybe a different theory suits my situation better: the self-fulfilling prophecy. It's possible that I'm so conscious of my "special talent" that I end up bringing it about myself. When my first love landed in Europe, I actually cautioned him about what could happen. Back then, though, he brushed the idea aside. "I'm so picky that I hardly ever really like a girl the way I like you," he wrote. Just a month later, he must have been quite surprised to learn that my dreadful gift stretched all the way across the Atlantic.

The day Ken revealed he was seeing Mary, I felt furious that I had allowed history to repeat itself yet again. I unleashed my anger on him. He countered that it made no sense to judge my future relationships (or my attempts at them) based on what had come before. I'm confident that one day a man will come along who won't find it so simple to get over me. Still, I can't just overlook the pattern and treat every instance as random chance, the way Ken suggested I should.

Whether there's any way to dodge what feels unavoidable, I honestly don't know. Every time I allow my hopes to overpower my superstition, there's a wreck, a fire, a collapse, and a brief stretch where I lose my ability to laugh. Even so, I'd rather take my chances as the girl who comes just before the girlfriend than surrender any possibility of finally ending my losing streak.

# On Being the Second Choice

There is a superstition I have long clung to: that if I imagine the worst possible outcome in vivid detail, I can somehow prevent it from happening. By rehearsing catastrophe in my mind, I believe I inoculate myself against it—as though fate, seeing that I've already anticipated the blow, will decide to spare me. Yet whatever protection this ritual offers, it has never extended to my emotional life. There, the disasters I dread seem to arrive regardless of how carefully I brace for them.

The particular heartbreak I return to again and again is this: I have a habit of becoming the "second choice." Time after time, I meet a man, feel that unmistakable spark of connection, and then watch as he forms a deep and lasting bond with someone else—often within weeks of our own beginning. It is as though I am merely the prelude to someone else's love story, the one who comes just before the person who truly matters.

The pattern established itself early. My first love ended our relationship because he was leaving to study in Europe, a reason I accepted as unavoidable, even noble. But almost immediately afterward, he became someone else's boyfriend—this despite having told me, only recently, that he still had feelings for me. The distance that had supposedly made our love impossible seemed to pose no obstacle at all when the right person came along. That person simply wasn't me.

I might have dismissed this as a single cruel coincidence, but it kept happening. The boy who gave me my first kiss chose another girl soon after. My friend Ken, with whom I shared an easy closeness that felt like the beginning of something more, turned his affection elsewhere. Then there was Brian, who followed the same script so precisely that I could almost have predicted it. Each of them, after a moment of genuine connection with me, went on to choose someone else.

And so I have begun to wonder whether the fault lies not in my luck but in my expectation. Have I become so acutely aware of this recurring outcome that I now unconsciously invite it? Perhaps my very vigilance—my constant watchfulness for the moment a man's attention drifts—creates the distance that pushes him away. The superstition I began with promised that imagining disaster might prevent it. But in matters of the heart, I fear the opposite may be true: that by rehearsing my abandonment so thoroughly, I have learned only how to make it come to pass.

# The Catalyst

There's a particular kind of ache that comes from being the person who prepares someone for love without ever being its recipient. I've come to recognize this pattern in my own life with the clarity of someone reading a familiar story—one where I already know I won't get the ending I want.

Let me explain what I mean.

Over and over again, I find myself sparking something real with a man. There's chemistry, conversation that stretches past midnight, the electric feeling of being truly seen. And then, almost as if on cue, he meets *her*—the one he was really meant for. I become the prologue to someone else's romance, the woman who somehow readies these men for the great loves of their lives without ever becoming one myself.

## Where It Began

I trace this back further than I probably should. My first love, at fifteen, spent months confiding in me about his uncertainties before finding the confidence to pursue the girl he eventually dated for three years. My first kiss came from a boy who, weeks later, would tell me I'd "helped him figure out what he wanted"—which turned out to be someone else entirely.

At the time, I chalked these up to the ordinary cruelties of adolescence. But the pattern didn't stop when I grew up. It followed me, refining itself, becoming almost surgical in its precision.

## Ken and Brian

The most recent instances still sting because they're so fresh.

There was Ken, whom I met at a mutual friend's gathering. We talked for hours that first night, and for weeks afterward, everything felt like the beginning of something. Then he met the woman he's now planning to marry. When he told me, he actually thanked me—said our conversations had made him realize he was ready to open up to someone.

And Brian. God, Brian. I really believed it might be different with him. But within a month of our growing closeness, he'd fallen for a colleague, and once again I found myself cast in the supporting role, the friend who somehow catalyzed a love that wasn't meant for me.

Two choices. Never *the* choice.

## The Psychology of It

I've spent enough sleepless nights analyzing this to have developed my own amateur theories, and some of them frighten me.

There's a concept called **catastrophic thinking**—the mental habit of assuming the worst possible outcome and treating it as inevitable. I recognize myself in this. From the moment I feel a connection forming, some part of my mind has already written the ending: *He'll leave. He'll find her. You're the catalyst, not the destination.*

But here's what unsettles me most. There's also the idea of the **self-fulfilling prophecy**—the way our expectations can shape our behavior in ways that make those very expectations come true. What if my certainty that I'll be the second choice is precisely what makes me one?

## The Uncomfortable Truth

I've started to wonder if my awareness of this pattern is no longer just observation—if it's become participation.

Perhaps I hold something back, some essential part of myself, because I'm bracing for the inevitable disappointment. Perhaps the men I connect with sense this reservation, this quiet resignation, and interpret it—correctly—as a signal that I'm not fully available for the kind of love they're looking for. Perhaps by treating myself as a catalyst, I've trained myself to *be* one.

The prophecy fulfills itself. The catastrophe I fear becomes the catastrophe I create.

I don't have a resolution to offer, no tidy epiphany that dissolves years of this recurring heartbreak. But I'm beginning to suspect that the pattern I've been passively enduring may be one I've been actively, if unconsciously, writing all along.

And if that's true—if my own certainty has been the architect of my loneliness—then maybe, just maybe, there's something I can change.

That possibility terrifies me. It also, for the first time, gives me hope.

# The Frisky Kitten

There was once a little kitten who lived at the edge of a quiet village. The moment the sun rose each morning, she would leap from her cozy basket, ready to explore the world. Everyone in the neighborhood called her Frisky, and the name suited her perfectly.

The way she chased butterflies through the garden made everyone smile. There was never a dull moment when Frisky was around. She would pounce on falling leaves, tumble through the tall grass, and dart between the flowerpots as if the entire yard belonged to her alone.

The children of the village adored her playful spirit. There, in the golden afternoon light, they would gather to watch Frisky perform her wild acrobatics. She would spring into the air, twist her tiny body, and land with the confidence of a seasoned dancer.

The best part of the day always came at dusk. There, curled up on a warm windowsill, Frisky would finally rest. The frisky energy that filled her days melted away into peaceful, contented purring.

There is something special about a creature so full of joy. The village would not be the same without Frisky, and everyone knew it. There, in her small and playful presence, was a reminder that happiness often comes in the tiniest, most frisky packages.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a first-person personal essay for The Frisky about being the girl guys date right before they meet "the one," exploring whether it's a self-fulfilling prophecy.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Bridesmaid of Relationships

I've been to four weddings in the last two years. At every single one, I knew the groom before he knew his bride. Actually, "knew" is putting it delicately. I dated three of them.

I am, apparently, the woman men date right before they marry someone else.

The first time it happened, I chalked it up to bad luck. Jake and I had six good months together before things fizzled the way things do. Eight months after we broke up, I saw the engagement announcement. He'd met her three weeks after me. *Three weeks.* I ate an entire sleeve of Thin Mints and told myself it was a fluke.

Then it happened again. And again. At this point, I'm considering putting it on my dating profile as a warning label, or maybe a selling point: *Date me and you'll find your wife within the year. Results not typical. Except they kind of are.*

## The Pattern I Can't Stop Seeing

Here's what haunts me about being the penultimate girlfriend: I keep wondering what she has that I don't. Or, more accurately, what I did that primed these men for her.

Did I do the emotional heavy lifting? Was I the one who taught them how to communicate, how to plan a real date, how to text back within a reasonable timeframe? Am I the relationship equivalent of a training bra—necessary, formative, and ultimately discarded for the real thing?

My best friend, who loves me but has no filter, put it bluntly over margaritas: "Maybe you fix them. And then they leave, all fixed, for someone else to enjoy."

I laughed. Then I went home and cried in the shower, which is the official crying venue of women who don't want to admit they're crying.

## The Question I'm Afraid to Answer

But here's what I've started to wonder, and it's uncomfortable enough that I've avoided writing it down until now: **What if I'm the one making this happen?**

What if I choose men I subconsciously know aren't right for me? What if I'm drawn to the almost-but-not-quite, the men who are emotionally *available adjacent*, because on some level, staying in the runner-up position is safer than actually winning?

Because think about it. If I'm always the woman before "the one," I never have to be "the one." I never have to be chosen fully. I never have to risk what happens when someone stays and it's *my* flaws, *my* baggage, *my* whole unedited self that they wake up next to for the next fifty years.

Being the almost-girlfriend is a strange kind of protection. I get the intimacy without the terror of permanence. And when they leave, I get to be the tragic figure, the one who "always gives too much," rather than the woman who has to ask herself the scarier question: *Did I ever actually let anyone all the way in?*

## Self-Fulfilling, Party of One

I've read enough psychology to be dangerous, and there's a concept that keeps circling my brain: we tend to create the reality we expect. If you walk into every relationship bracing for the exit, you telegraph it in a thousand tiny ways. You hold something back. You keep one foot near the door. You love with an asterisk.

Maybe these men could feel that. Maybe they sensed I was rehearsing our breakup even while we were still happy, and so they went looking for someone who wasn't already halfway gone. Someone present. Someone who wasn't protecting herself from being left by leaving first, emotionally, before anyone made it official.

That's the thing about a self-fulfilling prophecy—it doesn't feel like you're causing it. It feels like fate. It feels like *this always happens to me.* But "this always happens to me" is sometimes just the poetic way we describe the patterns we're too scared to interrupt.

## What I'm Trying Now

I don't have a triumphant ending here. I'm not writing this from my own wedding, smugly reformed. I'm writing it from my couch, dog on my lap, wondering if the next guy will meet his wife the second we stop returning each other's calls.

But I'm trying something new. I'm trying to stay. Not physically—I've always been good at staying physically. I mean the harder kind of staying. The kind where you let someone see the parts of you that aren't cute or curated. The kind where you stop auditioning for the role of "the girl he'll always remember" and start risking being "the girl he can't imagine leaving."

Maybe I'll always be the woman before the one. Maybe that's genuinely just bad luck and not a character flaw I can therapy my way out of.

But I'm starting to suspect that the woman these men eventually marry isn't luckier than me, or prettier, or more lovable.

I'm starting to suspect she's just braver.

And bravery, unlike bone structure, is something I can actually work on.

So if you've dated me and you're now blissfully engaged to someone you met a month after we ended: you're welcome. But also, quietly, to myself: *never again.*

The next time, I'm staying in the room.

---

*Do you have a dating pattern you can't seem to break? Tell us in the comments. Misery loves company, and company sometimes loves margaritas.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a confessional relationship column about repeatedly being men's "second choice" before they find the girl of their dreams, including specific examples with a first love who moved to Europe and friends named Ken and Brian.
counterfactuals.output:
# Always the Bridesmaid, Never the Dream

I've been someone's second choice so many times I've started to think it's my natural habitat. Like some women are born to be muses, and I was born to be the placeholder—the warm body someone holds onto until the real thing comes along.

Let me tell you about my first love. I'll call him David because that was his name and he moved to Europe, so what's he going to do, sue me from Prague?

We were together for two years. Two years of me learning his coffee order, memorizing his mother's birthday, teaching myself to like the obscure bands he worshipped. I thought we were building something. Then he got a job offer in Europe and asked me—asked me!—whether he should take it. I said yes because I loved him and wanted him to be happy, assuming "happy" included, you know, *me*.

He moved. Six months later, he was engaged to a woman he met at a wine bar in Prague. She's a translator who speaks four languages. I speak English and sarcasm. Guess who won.

Then there was Ken.

Ken and I dated for eight months, and I want to be fair to Ken because Ken was genuinely lovely in the way that makes the betrayal worse. He remembered things. He brought me soup when I was sick. But Ken had a "friend"—Rachel—who he swore was just a friend, the way men always swear about the woman they're actually saving themselves for. When Ken and I broke up, he waited a respectable *nine days* before making it official with Rachel. They're married now. There's a dog. The dog has an Instagram.

And Brian. Oh, Brian.

Brian actually *told* me I was his second choice, though not in those words, because men never use those words. What Brian said was: "You're the kind of woman a guy ends up with." *Ends up with.* As if I were a destination you reach only after the good exits are closed. Brian is now with a woman he describes as "the love of his life," which is a phrase he never once used about me in fourteen months of dating.

Here's what I've learned, sitting in the wreckage of being nobody's dream and everybody's rehearsal:

The problem was never that I wasn't enough. The problem was that I kept auditioning for roles that were already cast. I made myself into the runner-up so consistently that I stopped noticing I was the one handing out the silver medals.

I turned myself into whatever I thought each man needed—likable, low-maintenance, endlessly accommodating. I became so agreeable that I disappeared, and then I was shocked when men couldn't find me interesting enough to choose. You can't be someone's dream when you've sanded off every edge that makes you *you*.

So here's my confession, the real one underneath all the funny bitterness: I was my own second choice first. Every time. I picked their comfort over my needs, their potential over my reality, their someday over my right now.

David is married in Prague. Ken has a dog with better social media than me. Brian found his love of his life. And I'm here, finally understanding that I'd rather be alone than be anyone's placeholder ever again.

Because the next time someone chooses me, I want it to be because I *chose myself* first—loudly, unapologetically, and without waiting to see if anyone applauds.

The waiting room is closed. I'm not sitting in it anymore.

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a reflective essay opening with the idea that imagining catastrophes prevents them, then apply that superstition to a pattern of failed romances.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Rehearsal

I have always believed that if I imagine a disaster thoroughly enough, it will not come. This is my private superstition, the one I would never confess to a rational person. The plane will not fall from the sky if I have already pictured the shudder, the oxygen masks, the strange calm that supposedly descends. Catastrophe, in my cosmology, is a jealous thing. It wants to surprise you. Deny it that surprise, and it loses interest.

So I rehearse. I have rehearsed the deaths of everyone I love. I have imagined the phone call, the specific way my knees might give out, the odd details—who I would call first, whether I would remember to feed the cat. This is not morbidity. This is insurance. I am buying safety with the currency of dread, and for years I believed the exchange rate was fair.

It took me a long time to notice what I had been doing to the people I dated.

---

Consider the pattern. There was Daniel, who I was certain would grow bored of me. I saw it so clearly: the slow migration of his attention, the phone held slightly angled away, the eventual gentle speech about how he'd *changed.* I imagined it in such detail that I began, without quite deciding to, defending against it. I became less interesting on purpose, the way you might flinch before a blow that hasn't landed. I withheld the parts of myself I most wanted him to love, because loved things can be lost, and unloved things cannot. He grew bored. Of course he did. I had built him a boredom and moved him into it.

There was Maya, whose leaving I foresaw with such precision that I began packing her bags in my mind months before she'd given any sign. Every ambiguous silence I read as the overture to departure. I interrogated her contentment as though it were a lie. *You seem distant,* I would say, until distance was the only honest thing left for her to feel. I had imagined the catastrophe so vividly that I mistook my imagination for perception, and then for evidence, and then for cause.

Here is the flaw in my superstition, the one I refused to see: it works on planes because I have no influence over planes. My dread cannot reach into the engine. But love is not weather. Love is not a plane. I am *inside* it, my hands on something, and every catastrophe I rehearse, I also—quietly, faithfully—**build.**

---

The disasters I imagined did not stay imaginary. They were not warded off by my attention; they were summoned by it. I mistook a prophecy for a prevention. I thought I was the watchman on the wall. I was the arsonist with a very good alarm.

What frightens me now is not the pattern but the tenderness underneath it. Every time I imagined losing someone, I was, in my crooked way, loving them—loving them so much that I could not bear to be surprised by their loss. I wanted to control the grief in advance, to pre-pay it, so that the real thing, when it came, would find me already numb. And so I greeted every good thing already mourning it. I attended my relationships the way you attend a funeral: braced, formal, waiting for the part where you cry.

I don't know how to stop imagining catastrophes. The habit is old and it has, at least once, made me feel safe on a bad flight. But I am trying to learn a different superstition, one that runs the opposite direction. What if I imagined staying? What if I rehearsed the boring Tuesday twelve years from now, the shared grocery list, the argument that resolves? What if the thing I built with my attention were a future I actually wanted to walk into?

The plane, it turns out, was never the danger. The danger was that I loved the ground so much I kept practicing the fall.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I keep being the girl guys date right before they meet their real girlfriend. Turn my dating experiences into a witty, self-deprecating essay for a women's lifestyle site.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Girlfriend Whisperer

I have a gift. It's not a useful gift, like being able to parallel park on the first try or knowing exactly how much pasta to make for one person. My gift is this: I am the woman men date immediately before they meet the love of their lives.

I am the palate cleanser. The dating world's amuse-bouche. The final boss a man must defeat before unlocking the achievement of Serious Committed Relationship.

Let me walk you through the pattern, because at this point I've collected enough data to publish a peer-reviewed study.

There was Marcus, who told me he "wasn't looking for anything serious" over tapas we split because he was "trying to be smart with money." Three weeks after we stopped talking, he was Instagram-official with a woman whose face radiated the specific glow of someone who has never once split the tapas. They're engaged now. I know because the algorithm hates me.

Then came Daniel, who spent our six weeks together explaining that he had "trust issues" and "needed time." He needed time the way a caterpillar needs a cocoon—apparently to emerge as a fully transformed boyfriend for Rebecca, whom he met at a wedding roughly eleven days after ghosting me.

Do you see it? I am not a girlfriend. I am a training montage.

The most impressive part is my consistency. I don't just date the guys who *aren't ready*—I date them in the crucial final trimester of their un-readiness. I do the emotional labor. I sit through the therapy breakthroughs. I am the one who says "maybe you should call your dad" and "of course your ex was wrong about you." And then, like a doula of self-improvement, I deliver them—healthy, communicative, ready to love—directly into the arms of the next woman.

She gets the vows. I get the "thank you for making me a better person" text that arrives suspiciously close to their new anniversary.

For a while, I took this personally. I stared into mirrors asking what she had that I didn't, aside from impeccable timing and the good sense to not text back within four minutes. I wondered if I was fundamentally unlovable, or worse, *lovable in a way that inspires men to go love someone else.*

But I've made peace with my role. Somebody has to do it. Somewhere out there is a woman happily married to a man who learned to communicate his feelings, and she has no idea she owes it all to me and my willingness to date a guy whose apartment had one fork.

So this is my public service announcement to all future girlfriends: You're welcome. He's housebroken now. He knows what a "love language" is. He will remember your birthday, because he learned—the hard way, with me—that forgetting it has consequences.

I only ask one thing in return. When he tells you the sweet story about "the woman who came before, the one who really turned things around for him"—the one he speaks of with fondness and a faint sense of guilt—just know that she's out there, somewhere, splitting tapas with your future husband's predecessor's successor.

And she's fine. Really.

She's just waiting for the one guy who was ready *before* he met her.

He's got to exist. It's simple math. Somewhere, some man is right now finishing up his own training montage, being lovingly molded by a patient woman who will soon deliver him to *me.*

I'll send her a fruit basket.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a personal narrative about a dating pattern where every guy I connect with meets "the girl of his dreams" soon after, questioning whether it's coincidence or a self-fulfilling prophecy.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Bridesmaid of My Own Dating Life

There's a joke I've started telling at parties, the kind you rehearse until it sounds spontaneous. "I'm basically a lucky charm," I say, swirling my drink. "Date me for three months, and your soulmate appears like I summoned her."

People laugh. I laugh. And then I go home and stare at the ceiling, doing the math again.

Because it's happened five times now. Five.

---

There was Daniel, who I dated for a spring. We were casual, unlabeled, the kind of thing where you tell your friends "we'll see." Two months after we drifted apart, he met Priya at a mutual friend's barbecue. They're engaged now. I saw the ring on Instagram, a perfect emerald-cut testament to the fact that I was, apparently, the warm-up act.

Then Marcus. Then Theo. Then a guy whose name I've started leaving out of the story because it hurts the pacing. Each one, within a season of leaving my orbit, found *her*. The one. The girl they'd move across the country for, the one worth changing their entire personality for the wedding photos.

I'm not exaggerating for effect. I keep a mental ledger, and the ledger is undefeated.

---

The rational part of me knows this is confirmation bias wearing a trench coat. I'm collecting the hits and ignoring the misses. Somewhere out there are men I dated who are still single, still floundering, and I've conveniently forgotten them because they don't fit the tragic narrative I've built. The brain loves a pattern. It'll invent one if it has to.

But the other part of me—the 2 a.m. part—wonders something worse.

What if I'm doing it to myself?

---

Here's what I've never said out loud: I hold something back. Every time.

I go into these connections already braced for the ending. I keep one hand on the exit door, my emotional coat still on, ready to leave before I'm asked. I've told myself it's self-protection, maturity, not "coming on too strong." But what if what I'm actually doing is teaching these men how to leave? What if I show them, from day one, that I'm a place to pass through and not a place to stay?

Maybe I'm not the lucky charm. Maybe I'm the practice round. The girl who accidentally coaches them into readiness—teaches them what they want by demonstrating everything I'm afraid to fully offer—and then hands them, polished and prepared, to the woman who shows up unafraid.

The girl of their dreams gets a man who's finally figured out what he's looking for.

She just doesn't know he figured it out on me.

---

I brought this up to my sister once, and she said the thing sisters say: "Or maybe you keep choosing men who weren't ready, and their readiness had nothing to do with you at all."

I hated that answer because it made me smaller in the story. In my version, at least I have power—cursed power, but power. I'm the catalyst, the pivotal figure. In hers, I'm just a woman who kept picking half-finished people and taking their incompleteness personally.

Both versions might be true. That's the part I'm sitting with lately. That a pattern can be a coincidence *and* a message. That I could be both blameless and, somehow, complicit—not because I sabotage anyone, but because fear has a grammar, and mine spells "temporary."

---

I don't have a tidy ending. I'm not going to tell you I met someone who broke the streak, because I haven't. What I have is a new question I'm trying to ask instead of the old one.

The old question was: *Why does everyone find her but me?*

The new one is quieter, and it's aimed inward. *What would happen if, just once, I took the coat off? If I stayed in the room with my whole self, no exit strategy, no bracing?*

Maybe nothing. Maybe I'm still the lucky charm, and someday I'll toast a wedding I set in motion without meaning to.

But maybe the reason I keep meeting men right before they're ready is that I'm right there beside them—not quite ready myself. And the pattern I've been blaming on the universe has been standing in my mirror the whole time, wearing my face, keeping its coat on.

I'm working on it.

The coat, I mean.

One button at a time.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
